Russia has increased its oil exports to their highest level since the start of the full-scale war, but the value of those shipments has fallen to an 11-week low, Bloomberg reported. Russia is exporting an average of 3.65 million barrels of oil per day this year. Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries are one reason for the increase, as Moscow is being forced to sell abroad oil it can no longer process domestically. According to Bloomberg estimates, Ukraine has struck 17 Russian oil refineries since the beginning of November. The combined design capacity of the first 15 facilities alone accounts for more than half of Russia’s total refining capacity. The surge in Russian exports is adding to the global oil oversupply and putting further downward pressure on prices. Brent crude has already fallen nearly 25% from its late-October peak. Meanwhile, the gross value of Russia’s seaborne oil exports fell to $1.94 billion last week, its lowest level in 11 weeks.

Visioner BIG | 🇺🇦 🇳🇴 ‼️ ‼️ Ukraine and Norway are working to integrate Ukrainian-made missiles directly into the NASAMS air defense system, a move that could significantly expand Kyiv’s interceptor production and reduce its dependence on foreign missile supplies. Norwegian Defense Minister Tore Sandvik announced that Ukrainian forces have already begun operating the jointly developed DESNA air defense system. Norway has purchased and delivered several units in recent months. DESNA combines Ukrainian launchers and RK-2PZ surface-to-air missiles developed by the Luch Design Bureau with fire control technology from Norway’s Kongsberg. The RK-2PZ, presented at MSPO 2026, is based on the Barrier anti-tank missile and is also used in the modernized Strela-10 system known as Rif. The next step is adapting Ukrainian missiles for use with NASAMS. Integrating domestically produced interceptors into NASAMS could be an important development for Ukraine’s air defenses. It would allow Kyiv to combine established Western radar and fire control technology with missiles manufactured at home, potentially lowering costs and increasing available ammunition. With Russia continuing large-scale drone and missile attacks, expanding interceptor production remains essential to sustaining Ukraine’s air defense network.
